name: Social Scheduling Tools
tagline: A hosted tool for drafting, queueing and auto-publishing posts across social accounts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The scheduler itself is a beginner exercise: a table of posts, a due timestamp, a worker that fires on a cron. An agent will hand you a working queue with a calendar view in an afternoon and it will feel like you won. The gap is everything downstream of the queue: each platform wants its own OAuth app, its own review process, its own media upload dance, and some of them want money or a business account before they let you post at all. Bluesky and Mastodon will work in an hour. Instagram, TikTok, X and LinkedIn are where your weekend goes, and they can break your build without asking.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you write a post once, pick target accounts and a time, and a background worker publishes it through each platform's API.
requirements: A developer app plus OAuth credentials for every platform you want to post to
A machine or small VPS that actually stays awake to run the scheduler
Business or professional accounts for Instagram and Facebook publishing
Tolerance for API terms changing under you
whatYouLose: Platform integrations that someone else maintains when the APIs change
Reliable retries, rate limit handling and failure alerts you did not have to think about
Preview rendering that matches what each network actually shows
Analytics on how the posts performed
Mobile access and posting from your phone unless you host it publicly
moatNotes: The product is not the calendar, it is being an approved app in good standing with a half dozen platforms that dislike third party posting tools.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the boring middle layer is real work that never ends. Every network changes its auth flow, media limits or approval rules on its own schedule, and a paid tool absorbs that churn silently. If you post to two or three friendly networks for yourself, the DIY version is genuinely fine and cheaper. If you manage client accounts on Instagram and TikTok and need someone to blame when a post fails to go out, you pay.
notes: Building the queue is a Saturday; keeping five platform integrations alive is a subscription you pay in your own time.
prompt:
Build a local-first social media scheduler as a single Node.js project. No accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20 with TypeScript, Fastify for the HTTP server
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/scheduler.db
- Server-rendered HTML with Fastify views and plain CSS, plus a little vanilla JS. No React.
- node-cron for the dispatch loop
- All credentials read from .env via dotenv, with a .env.example committed and .env gitignored

Data model:
- accounts: id, platform, handle, credentials_json, enabled
- posts: id, body, media_path (nullable), scheduled_at (UTC ISO), status (draft, queued, sent, failed), created_at
- targets: id, post_id, account_id, status, remote_id, error, attempts

Features in scope:
- Compose page: textarea with per-platform character counters, optional single image upload stored in ./data/media, account checkboxes, datetime picker treated as local time and stored as UTC
- Queue page: upcoming posts grouped by day, plus edit, duplicate, delete, and send now
- A simple week calendar view of scheduled posts
- Dispatcher: cron every minute, picks queued targets due now, publishes, retries failed targets up to 3 times with exponential backoff, writes errors to the row
- Publisher adapters behind one interface: publish(account, post) returning a remote id. Implement Bluesky (app password) and Mastodon (access token) for real. Implement a Dry Run adapter that logs to a file. Stub X, LinkedIn and Instagram adapters that throw a clear not-configured error and document in the README exactly what developer app and approval each one needs.
- CLI script: npm run send-due, so the dispatcher can also run from an external cron

Out of scope, do not build: analytics, teams, AI caption generation, link shortening, image editing, threads or carousels, approval workflows.

Deliver a README with setup steps, how to add an account, timezone behaviour, and a blunt section on which platforms will not work without their own developer program. Include a seed script that creates a Dry Run account and two sample posts so the whole loop is demonstrable with zero credentials.
